title: The Trench
hookLine: Salman the Persian suggests a trench, and all dig, the Prophet ﷺ among them, hungry (33:9–11)

cards: After Uhud, the news gets worse. Mecca has gathered allies from across Arabia. The biographers put the army at about ten thousand, coming to finish Medina for good, and the city's fighters at maybe three thousand.
There's no wall. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ calls his companions together to plan, and the ideas go around the circle. Then a man speaks up who isn't from Mecca, or Medina, or Arabia at all.
He's a Persian, a former slave, and he says: where I come from, when we're besieged, we dig a trench. The early biographers say no one in Arabia had fought that way before.

teach.b: The man was Salman al-Farisi, Salman the Persian. As a young man he had left his home in Persia searching for the truth, traveled through Syria, been sold into slavery, and ended up in Medina, where he became Muslim.
The Prophet took his idea, and the Muslims of the city dug. The trench ran across Medina's open northern side, where horsemen could charge. It was winter, and cold.
Food was so short that, Jabir says in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet had a stone bound against his stomach to quiet the hunger.
Another report there says he carried earth until the dust covered his belly, and chanted with the diggers as they worked.
When they hit a rock no one could break, they called him, and he took the pickaxe himself and struck until it crumbled. Then the army arrived, and stopped. Horses can't jump a deep ditch.
The siege dragged on for weeks.
The Qur'an describes how it felt inside the city: the enemy came at you from above and below, eyes grew wild, hearts rose into throats, and the believers were shaken hard.
Then, it says, God sent a wind, and hosts they could not see.
The biographers say a cold, violent wind tore through the enemy camp at night, overturning pots and blowing out fires, and the great army packed up and left.
Muslims remember it as the battle of the Trench, or of the Confederates, al-Ahzab, the name of the surah that tells it. And they remember who had the idea.

how: Muslims remember the battle of the Trench through Surah al-Ahzab, and Salman al-Farisi is honored as an example of a seeker from far away, embraced by the community.

o: a wall of stone built around Medina
a ditch dug to stop an army's horsemen
a dry riverbed where the armies fought

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the trench was an old Arab way of fighting
the early biographers say it was new in Arabia, an idea Salman brought from Persia.
the Prophet dug and carried earth himself
Sahih al-Bukhari says the dust covered his belly.
the siege ended in a great battle at the trench
the Qur'an says God sent a wind and unseen hosts, and the army left.

games.q: you're planning to defend a city with no wall. a newcomer from far away suggests something no one here has ever done. what do you do?
o: ask him to prove it first.
games.why: the Prophet took Salman's idea, and the Muslims of Medina dug. the army of ten thousand couldn't cross.

practice: Think of a problem you've been stuck on, and of who you haven't asked: the new person at work, someone from another country or generation, a kid, someone whose ways are nothing like yours.
Imagine asking them and actually listening, the way the Prophet listened to Salman, then picture everyone digging together.

wordCard.voice: The Trench. Salman the Persian's idea, dug by the Muslims of Medina, the Prophet among them, that held back an army of ten thousand. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the trench. classical Arabic lexicons list it as a word taken from Persian.

carryVoice: Your line: dig together. Everyone with a shovel, the Prophet too, hungry and cold. See you tomorrow.
